item.title: Organizational strengthening resources for nonprofits
item.description:
Nonprofits today are navigating challenging and uncertain times — funding cuts, shifting political headwinds, digital and physical security threats, and, in some cases, hard conversations about organizational sustainability. This list gathers free resources, funded in part by the Hewlett Foundation, that are available to any nonprofit looking for support with strategic transitions, legal assistance, financial resilience, digital security, and board governance.

GLOBAL

Access Now provides digital security support for organizations around the world. Reach the team at help@accessnow.org.

Civic Strength Partners helps organizations plan for strategic transitions, mergers and partnerships, restructuring, and protection of assets. Support includes matchmaking, transition preparation support, and merger accompaniment and implementation guidance. Expertise includes legal, governance, finance, strategy, communications, HR, and responsible asset disposition. Reach out here.

PILnet (Global Network of Public Interest Law) offers pro bono access to legal expertise to meet the needs of nonprofits, and to strengthen organizations working for a more just and equitable world. Get legal assistance here.

The Cyrus R. Vance Center for International Justiceengages lawyers globally to support civil society and an ethically active legal profession. It offers legal assistance to organizations working to protect the environment, human rights, institutional integrity and others. Reach out here.

US DOMESTIC

Democracy Protection Networkprovides assistance with physical security, cybersecurity, crisis communications, and legal advice and representation for organizations whose issue areas are impacted by shrinking democratic space. Apply here.

Nonprofit GPShelps nonprofit leaders make well-informed decisions and navigate business model risks to keep their mission alive, even in disruptive times. It draws on the grounded experience of Nonprofit Financial Commons and BDO’s Nonprofit and Grantmaker Advisory practice, as well as the tools at StrongNonprofits.org and other collaborating networks, offering:

  • Publicly available resources
  • Peer convenings and webinars
  • A free, confidential helpline for financial and organizational management

Sign up here to receive their latest updates and resources.

NGO-ISAC helps strengthen the security of nonprofits by bringing them together in a collaborative community where they can share information, learn from one another, and stay ahead of emerging threats to civil society. Nonprofits can join here.

Democracy Notes is a trade publication and field-support organization serving the U.S. democracy space. Its goal is to connect people and share sector-specific information through field news, peer-learning cohorts, events, and research. They recently launched a Wellbeing Resource Library.

Conservation Capacity Project offers free webinars, curated resources, well-being support, and one-on-one coaching and technical assistance to conservation nonprofits and Tribes. To access the free offerings and organizational coaching from experts in areas such as fundraising, communications, digital security, and strategic partnerships, join the mailing list here.

BoardSource

All Hewlett grantees have access to an annual BoardSource membership, which includes hundreds of governance tools and resources, Ask the Expert service, a dedicated community for grantees and board members to connect and collaborate, and a comprehensive on-demand training program. Set up your BoardSource membership by completing this form.

The post Organizational strengthening resources for nonprofits appeared first on Hewlett Foundation.

item.title: Building belonging and confidence through music
item.description:
Like many summer camps, mornings at Cazadero Music Camp in Northern California start with reveille. Unlike most camps, Caz often remixes the classic wake-up call — maybe with a brass ensemble, or oboes impersonating bagpipes, or banging on pots and pans with kitchen utensils. Since almost everyone on site, from staff to students, is a musician, the possibilities are endless. It’s the first of many musical moments Cazadero campers experience every day.  

Next year, Cazadero celebrates its 70th anniversary. Since becoming a nonprofit in the 1990s, the camp has inspired nearly 30,000 student musicians, supported by a decades-long partnership with the Hewlett Foundation. Located in a redwood forest, Caz welcomes kids ages 9 to 18 to make music while enjoying classic summer camp fun. Campers return year after year to grow as musicians and make lifelong friends, and many return as alumni to serve as staff.  

“At Hewlett, we believe that connecting Bay Area communities to the performing arts begins by bringing those experiences to our youngest neighbors,” said Tom DeCaigny, Program Officer on Hewlett’s Performing Arts team.  

Cazadero’s Executive Director Emily Wainacht knows the benefits of youth arts programs personally; she’s a Cazadero alum who credits the camp with her lifelong commitment to music.  

“There was a period when I was on the verge of quitting music entirely,” recalls Wainacht. “Caz changed that. Surrounded by an incredible community of peers and inspiring teachers who brought such joy and excitement to playing, that short time at camp gave me the purpose and drive to keep going all year long.”

Wainacht spent five years at Caz as a camper before returning as a counselor and eventually becoming Executive Director. But this summer was unlike any she’d experienced before.  

A storm and a deadline 

In December 2025, Cazadero was hit by a major storm. On Christmas Eve, Wainacht started receiving alarming texts from Camp Director Carolyn Niehaus-Owen, including photos of devastating damage. Cazadero is located in one of the rainiest parts of California, so the camp is used to storms, landslides, and floods — but nothing had compared to this.  

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Cazadero Music Camp (@cazmusiccamp)

“I went up shortly after Christmas…the pictures couldn’t even do it justice. There were branches everywhere, and the force of the branches falling and the wind had caused punctures to decks and incredible amounts of damage,” said Wainacht. “It was awful to see and hard to imagine it looking like Caz again.”  

Already halfway through the off-season, she and her team only had a few months to get camp ready. It was a big job. Still, the team was determined to open for their full 2026 camp season. “We immediately started making plans and figuring out the next steps,” said Wainacht. “Always with the goal in mind of safely opening for our first program in May. That was always the goal for us.” 

To meet that target, the team started rebuilding immediately. It was an intensive process, involving a lot of logistics between the City of Berkeley — which is Cazadero’s landlord — insurance companies, and contractors. Slowly and carefully, they started chipping away at the damage and debris while sharing regular updates with their camp community online.  

Things started feeling more normal by the time Cazadero hosted its volunteer weekend in April — an annual pre-summer tradition that took on a new meaning in the wake of the storm damage. Volunteers helped with standard opening tasks, like setting up bed frames and tarps for tents, and that’s when it was finally clear they would open as scheduled. The turnout was also a reminder of how many people care about Caz, with alumni, former staff, and neighbors all showing up to help.  

A summer of music, against the odds 

This summer, Cazadero welcomed 645 campers and employed 147 staff, none of whom would have been able to attend if camp wasn’t ready to open. Campers spent several hours a day in music classes, learning new pieces in only a few days, studying under different conductors, and performing concerts every week for a live audience. All of them share one thing: a commitment to their craft. As one camper described it: “Everyone speaks the same language. Not the language of English, Spanish, or French, but the language of music.” 

Wainacht also pointed to the broader value of sleepaway camp itself, whether campers spend their days studying instruments, playing sports, or simply soaking up the summer sun.  

“In a world increasingly driven toward isolation and screens, camp gives young people this incredible opportunity to connect and collaborate together, in person. And we’re in this canyon in a redwood forest with no cell reception,” she said. “They’re fully present in the work of the camp and the communities that they are building.” 

DeCaigny said, “Whether someone dreams of a career in music or simply enjoys playing as a hobby, I have seen firsthand the impact Caz has on campers. It shows the power of music to bring people together while helping young people become more creative, confident, and connected to their communities.” 

Cazadero just closed out another successful summer. Looking back, Wainacht can recall countless memories that made the long hours of cleanup and complicated logistics more than worth it, but one in particular stands out: a shy student whose stage fright was so severe he ran off stage during an earlier school concert. This summer, he joined Cazadero’s jazz ensemble and conquered his fears by opting to perform not once but twice at the weekly concert.  

“At Caz, he found that joy in music again.”

item.title: Equipping students to be active participants in our democracy
item.description:
When student Landon F. set out to understand why so few of his peers engaged in community activities and other forms of civic life, he found an answer he didn’t expect: His school, Frewsburg Central High School in western New York, offered no civics course. He decided to change that.

Landon organized a student petition committee, cultivated teacher advocates, and eventually presented to his school board. With support from a Carnegie Youth Fellowship through iCivics — a nonprofit that helps schools and students all over America engage in civics education — Landon also interviewed students from across the country about their civics education.

“Hearing how people from all over different parts of the country have different civic experiences is crazy to me,” he said. “You would think there would be a standard to this — civic education requirements, voting, basic engagement, etc. It really makes me think about what we need to do differently.”

Landon’s school isn’t an outlier. In the U.S., civics is often only a single semester in high school, if it’s taught at all, despite research showing that 92% of Americans think civic education is important for our country’s success. Research shows that strong civic learning encourages students to volunteer in their community, advocate for causes they care about, discuss local issues at home, and vote in elections. That’s the foundation that iCivics, a grantee of the Hewlett Foundation’s Education program, is working inside and outside the classroom to give every student in America.

Founded by former Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O’Connor, iCivics develops free, high-quality educational games, curriculum and classroom tools that help young people understand and participate in democratic life. Every year, its resources reach 9 million students and are used by teachers in 80% of U.S. counties, across school size, in urban and rural districts, and in red, blue, and purple states.

“Civic education is one of the most powerful, underutilized levers we have for protecting human agency and constitutional democracy as the world shifts around us,” said iCivics CEO Louise Dubé. “We must act now to strengthen it on a national scale and reposition it at the center of our education system.”

iCivics designs its curricula to meet students where they are. Its Through Inquiry curriculum has students lead their own learning by asking compelling questions, evaluating primary sources, and completing a capstone project that brings what they’ve learned to life. And because curriculum is only as effective as the teachers who deliver it, iCivics also builds educator capacity through professional development offerings ranging from full courses to immediately actionable workshops.

Beyond curricular and teacher supports, games from iCivics guide students through the democratic process, ensure students understand the history of our nation and the rights they enjoy, demonstrate the consequences of their decisions, and help them develop the civil discourse skills they need to navigate diverse perspectives.

  • In the game Neighborhood Good students step into a fictional neighborhood and pick a local challenge to tackle — such as decreasing food waste or supporting a local animal shelter. They meet with their neighbors, listen to their concerns and ideas, and use what they learn to build a plan to help. Students then see how working together benefits the community’s residents.
  • In Investigation Declaration, students become special agents tasked with redrawing connections between Enlightenment ideas and the Declaration of Independence and identifying how those ideas spread across the Atlantic World over the course of a century.

According to Johns Hopkins research, iCivics resources build students’ critical thinking capacities. They also develop their ability to communicate, collaborate, evaluate information, and be creative — skills that will set them up to succeed in the economy of the future.

After using iCivics resources, students often voice things like: “I didn’t realize I had a role in this.” Teachers share that iCivics games and other tools also encourage students who once hesitated to participate to now raise their hands, engage in class conversations, and dive into their curriculum with excitement.

“No matter what plans students have for life after high school — whatever their career plans, however they may continue their education — all students will be members of communities where they will need agency to raise their voices and make an impact. Civics teaches skills, knowledge, and disposition that will be needed by all,” said Shannon Salter, iCivics Educator Network Teacher.

iCivics is also working outside of classrooms alongside advocates and policymakers to ensure more students are taught these skills. Their CivxNow project, the nation’s largest cross-partisan coalition working to prioritize civic learning in the United States, has encouraged more than 30 states to adopt over 50 civic education policies that teach students interactive and relevant K-12 political participation, civil discourse, and how to engage over disagreements.

At the national level, iCivics and the CivxNow coalition helped triple funding for K–12 civic education programs in the 2023 fiscal year, from $7.75 million to $23 million.

“With civic learning in and out of the classroom and iCivics’ resources and curricula at teachers’ and students’ fingertips, our nation’s young people are better positioned to contribute to the future of their communities, and help build and sustain a durable democracy that works for us all, across our differences,” said Melissa Chabran, Hewlett Foundation Education Program Officer.

The post Equipping students to be active participants in our democracy  appeared first on Hewlett Foundation.
